messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar, a 41-year-old Middle Eastern construction worker who lives alone, first learned what danger sounded like as a boy in his family’s apartment, where he would hear his mother’s voice rising, a door slamming, and then the dull thud of his father hitting her against the wall. He witnessed those episodes only in fragments, because some moments are etched into him with startling force — the pattern on the kitchen tile, his mother’s hand on the sink, his father’s shoes moving toward her — while other parts are blank, as if the tape has gaps. When he tries to remember the scene deliberately, Omar finds he cannot pull it up in a smooth way; it comes back instead like a series of photographs, harsh and frozen, and that broken quality makes the memory feel more ominous. He has come to dread anything that resembles the charged atmosphere of those nights, especially confrontation, and he is especially unsettled by police presence, which he links to the moments when adults outside the home seemed to arrive only after things had already gone too far. Even talking about the future can catch him off guard, because planning ahead stirs a sense that something bad could interrupt it at any moment. In those situations he feels it in his body immediately — his chest tightens, his muscles brace, and he becomes hyperaware of the people around him, studying faces and body language for signs of threat before he even knows he is doing it.

Over the years, Omar has managed this by slipping away mentally. At work on construction sites, where foremen and subcontractors regularly press for quick decisions and disagreements can flare around schedules or money, he often drifts off into a world of his own when tensions rise. If a supervisor starts talking about next month’s bids or a client asks what the project will look like after completion, Omar’s mind can go somewhere distant, and he avoids adding his own thoughts so he will not be drawn into argument. He has also fallen into the habit of dwelling on how he used to be before the violence in his home, when he felt more open and less guarded, as though the old version of himself were someone he lost and might never recover. These habits bring short-lived relief, but they keep the memory close in another way: when he drifts off or turns inward, the old scenes return in flashes, and the photographs in his mind become harder to shake. Afterward, he is even more likely to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, which means he stays silent with co-workers, steps back from family discussions, and leaves before tensions can build. That avoidance also preserves his sense that the world is dangerous, because the less he speaks up, the more he watches, and the more he watches, the more he sees possible threat in a tightened jaw, a prolonged pause, or someone taking longer than expected to answer a text or return to the job trailer.

The old memory and the present-day threat have begun to feed one another. When Omar is waiting for a foreman to appear, or when a police car passes the site, his body reacts before he can think; he feels the same sharp alarm that once filled the apartment, and that physical surge pushes him back into his head. Then the memory comes in pieces — impossible to hold onto, but impossible to dismiss — and he is left with the sense that something terrible is about to happen just out of view. The more he scans faces and body language for danger, the more certain he becomes that he is missing some crucial sign, and that certainty makes him retreat further into fantasy and silence. That retreat, in turn, leaves him less able to face reminders directly, so the future itself starts to feel threatening. Even ordinary talk about what work will look like in a few weeks can make him tense and withdrawn, as if forward planning invites the next blow. He has noticed that when he loses himself in these mental escapes, he later struggles even more to recall the event in an orderly way, and the blank spaces seem to widen around the vivid images.

Recently, the strain has become hard to hide. On site, a small dispute over a delivery delay left Omar shaking and unable to concentrate, and he spent the rest of the day watching people’s faces instead of the work. He left early, drove home in silence, and sat alone avoiding his phone because he did not want to hear anyone suggest he should “just move on” or discuss what comes next. What brought him to seek help was the realization that his life has narrowed around these moments of alarm and retreat, and that he is becoming more isolated in both work and relationships. Omar says he is most afraid that if he keeps living this way, he will never feel safe enough to build anything lasting, but he still hopes that if he can understand why these memories remain so vivid and so broken, he might finally stop reacting as though the violence is happening again.
